subject: Chemistry
title: Cadmium Yellow: Bright and Banned
description: A micro-lesson that makes Cadmium Yellow: Bright and Banned usable.

hook.text: Cadmium yellow is one of the brightest, most lightfast yellows ever made. It's also toxic and increasingly restricted.

buildup.text: Cadmium sulfide (CdS) produces intense yellow. Adding selenium shifts it to orange and red—a whole color family.

discovery.text: Monet, Van Gogh, and Matisse all used cadmium colors. Their paintings have kept their brilliance for over a century.

twist.text: Sweden proposed banning cadmium pigments in 2014. Artists protested—no synthetic alternative matches their color and stability.

climax.text: The EU exempted artist paints from the ban. Cadmium is too toxic for mass products but irreplaceable for fine art.

punchline.text: Toxic but irreplaceable. Some colors are too brilliant to have safe alternatives.

quiz.question: Why haven't cadmium pigments been fully replaced in artist paints?
options: No synthetic alternative matches their color intensity and lightfastness
Cadmium pigments are actually non-toxic in small amounts
Artists haven't been informed about the health risks

details.summary: Cadmium sulfide produces an intense yellow that became a favorite of Impressionist and Post-Impressionist painters including Monet and Van Gogh. Modern environmental regulations have restricted cadmium pigment use due to the heavy metal's toxicity and persistence in ecosystems.
details.whyItMatters: Cadmium yellow illustrates the tension between artistic brilliance and environmental responsibility. The push to ban cadmium pigments in Europe has driven development of new safer alternatives.
takeaways: Cadmium sulfide's band gap produces a vivid, lightfast yellow
Van Gogh and Monet relied heavily on cadmium yellows in their work
EU regulations restrict cadmium in consumer products since 2011

faq.question: Why did Impressionist painters prefer cadmium yellow over older alternatives?
faq.answer: Cadmium yellow offered exceptional lightfastness, intense brightness, and excellent opacity that earlier yellows like chrome yellow or gamboge could not match. It did not darken or fade with age, making it ideal for the Impressionists' outdoor painting practice.

faq.question: Is cadmium yellow still available for artists to purchase today?
faq.answer: Yes, cadmium pigments remain available for professional artists in most countries. EU restrictions target consumer products and industrial uses, not fine art supplies. However, many paint manufacturers now offer cadmium-free alternatives that closely match the color and lightfastness.
